Neonates of the Roughtail skate (Bathyraja trachura) emerge from their egg cases at a total length of 20 centimeters [Lb = 20 centimeters]. This modest birth size places them among the smaller-bodied offspring within the deep-sea skate assemblage of the North Pacific. The yolk sac provides the initial nutritional reserves for the pup, and the timing of yolk-sac resorption marks the onset of independent foraging. Growth trajectories in this species have been estimated through mark-recapture studies and vertebral banding patterns, revealing a slow but steady increase in body dimensions over the first several years of life. The ultimate total length attained by adults is 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters], a value that represents the asymptotic size inferred from the largest individuals captured during deepwater trawl surveys. This maximum recorded length is consistent across most of the species' geographic range, although slight regional variation has been noted. The length-weight relationship indicates that an individual reaching this asymptotic size would achieve an ultimate wet weight of 5200 grams [Wwi = 5200 grams], calculated from the length-mass conversion. This substantial body mass underscores the species' position as a moderately large skate within the Bathyraja genus.

Puberty in Roughtail skate is attained at a distinct total length that differs between the sexes. For females, the total length at puberty is 79.6 centimeters [Lp = 79.6 centimeters], while males reach maturity at a slightly smaller size of 74.1 centimeters [Lp = 74.1 centimeters]. This sexual dimorphism in size at maturation is a common pattern among elasmobranchs and likely reflects the differing energetic demands associated with egg production versus sperm competition. These length thresholds were determined through histological examination of gonadal tissue in specimens collected across the continental slope, where the species is most frequently encountered. The attainment of these sizes represents a crucial life-history transition, after which individuals shift from a purely somatic growth phase to one that includes significant reproductive investment. Field observations indicate that post-pubertal females are frequently encountered with developing ovarian follicles, confirming that the length-based estimate of maturity aligns well with functional reproductive status. Males at 74.1 centimeters typically exhibit fully calcified claspers and active spermatogenesis.

The time required to reach puberty is strongly influenced by the ambient temperature of the deep-sea environment. At a relatively cold water temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], which is typical of the depths this species inhabits, the estimated time since birth at puberty for females is approximately 24.7 years [tp = approximately 24.7 years]. This protracted period reflects the extremely low metabolic rates and reduced food availability characteristic of deep-sea habitats. The extended juvenile period is a common trait among deep-sea skates and is associated with low natural mortality rates in the adult stage.

Reproductive output in Roughtail skate appears to be modest, consistent with the pattern of low fecundity observed in many deep-sea elasmobranchs. Based on data from the congeneric species Bathyraja interrupta, which provides a useful ecological analogue, the annual reproductive rate can be estimated. Females are believed to produce approximately six to nine pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately six to nine pups per litter] following successful mating. Given that reproduction likely occurs on an annual cycle at the prevailing deep-sea temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], the frequency of reproductive events is approximately one litter each year [F_R_i = approximately one litter each year]. This low reproductive rate, combined with the late age at maturity, renders the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation. The total lifespan of the Roughtail skate under these cold-temperature conditions has been estimated at 36 years [am = 36 years], based on longevity records from growth ring analysis of vertebral centra at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. This extended lifespan, also recorded at 4 °C [T = 4 °C], further reinforces the slow life-history strategy that characterizes this deep-water skate.

Ecologically, the Roughtail skate occupies a benthic niche on the continental slope, typically at depths between 800 and 2800 meters, where the near-constant temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C] governs its physiological processes. This cold thermal regime is a primary driver of the species' remarkably slow pace of life, contributing to both the protracted maturation period and the extended maximum longevity. The species is an opportunistic predator, feeding largely on benthic invertebrates such as shrimps, amphipods, and polychaetes, as well as small demersal fishes. Comparative analyses within the family Arhynchobatidae suggest that Bathyraja trachura exhibits one of the highest longevity estimates relative to body size, a trait that is evolutionarily linked to the stable, low-productivity environment of the deep sea. The relatively small litter size and infrequent reproduction further emphasize the trade-off between current reproductive effort and the maintenance of somatic condition over a long lifetime. Interestingly, the pronounced difference in size at maturity between sexes—with females maturing at 79.6 centimeters [Lp = 79.6 centimeters] compared to 74.1 centimeters [Lp = 74.1 centimeters] in males—aligns with patterns observed in other deepwater skates where larger females may benefit from increased space for egg case development in the oviducal gland. This dimorphism, combined with the fact that females reach puberty nearly three and a half years later than males, suggests that the reproductive strategy of Bathyraja trachura involves a significant time investment in achieving a size that maximizes fecundity, even at the cost of delaying first pupping.
